See TAIL OS run on a Linux machine with QEMU — no board, no toolchain, no build. Every
command from step 2 on was run against the published image with QEMU 10.2, and the output
shown is what it printed.

You need a Linux machine with at least 2 CPUs and enough free disk for QEMU and TAIL OS. On
Ubuntu 24.04 the QEMU packages below take 580 to 970 MiB, depending on what is already
installed; TAIL OS takes about 300 MiB more, or about 600 MiB if you also follow
[Without the launcher](#without-the-launcher), which keeps its own copy.

QEMU emulates the Raspberry Pi 3's four CPU cores. It runs best with 4 or more CPUs (`nproc`
counts them) and more slowly with 2. With 1 it is slower still: on our machine the shell came
up in about 13 seconds and `python /hello.py` took about 18, and timings vary from run to run.

```bash
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y qemu-system-arm qemu-utils
```

Download the launcher, then run it:

```bash
curl -O https://tail-os.com/downloads/run_tailos_qemu.sh
chmod +x run_tailos_qemu.sh
./run_tailos_qemu.sh
```

The launcher downloads the kernel and data disk into `~/.cache/tailos/`, checks each
against the published `SHA256SUMS`, and boots them. The first run downloads about 15 MiB,
which unpacks to about 263 MiB in the cache. It shows no progress while it does: after
`fetching https://tail-os.com/downloads/tail_disk.img.gz` nothing more appears until the
download, unpacking and check are done. Later runs start from the cache, which the launcher
replaces only when a new image is published, so booting again is just `./run_tailos_qemu.sh`.
Each run still fetches the small `SHA256SUMS` to check for a new image, so it needs the
network.

Boot takes a few seconds: about 1 on our machine, with 4 CPUs and QEMU 10.2, and about 8 on
a 2-CPU cloud machine with Ubuntu 24.04's QEMU 8.2. A slower machine takes longer, and the log can pause for a while, longest just before the line ending
`FAT File System Server initialized`, but it has not hung.

Before the shell starts, the launcher prints a few lines of its own, then TAIL OS prints a banner
beginning `TailOS  aarch64 / rpi3  build` and about 40 lines of boot log, each tagged `[STRT]`,
`[ OK ]` or `[INFO]`. The two `[INFO]` lines where the wifi and bt expander
`did not acknowledge` are expected: QEMU's emulated firmware ignores that request. Lines
from different services can arrive out of timestamp order. When the shell starts you see:

```
TAIL OS Shell (tsh)
Type 'exit' to quit, 'help' for built-in commands.

/$
```

To leave QEMU at any point, press **Ctrl-A**, then a lowercase **x**. QEMU prints `QEMU: Terminated`
and you are back at your own shell.

Each command below answers within a second or two, and `python /hello.py` within several
seconds. Wait for the `/$` prompt before typing the next command; text typed while a command
is still running appears twice.

```
/$ help
Built-in commands:
  exit [code]    - Exit the shell (optionally with exit code)
  cd [dir]       - Change current working directory
  pwd            - Print current working directory
  echo [-n] args - Print arguments ($VAR expanded)
  export K=V     - Set (and export) an environment variable
  cat <file...>  - Display file contents
  clear          - Clear the terminal screen
  history        - Show command history
  mkdir <dir...> - Create directories
  touch <file..> - Create empty files
  test EXPR      - Evaluate a conditional expression
  [ EXPR ]       - Same as 'test', with a closing ']'
  true / false   - Yield success / failure status
  help           - Show this help message

Scripting: 'tsh <file> [args]' runs a script; if/while/for, &&, ||,
';', $?, $1..$@ and '#!/rfs/tsh' shebangs are supported.

External commands are executed as separate processes.
```

```
/$ ls /
etc       hello.py  usr
/$ ls /usr/bin
bluetoothctl    isrfat          netstat         route           waitfor
cp              kill            ping            shutdown        wcetdump
dhcp            list-root-long  ps              sleep           which
fetch           logview         python          time            wifi
find            ls              reboot          top
grep            mv              rm              vi
```

```
/$ ps
PID    PPID   STATE      THREADS  NAME
0      -      LOADING    0        startup
1      -      RUNNING    11       kernel
2      -      RUNNING    2        uart_pl011
3      -      RUNNING    3        log_server
4      -      RUNNING    1        pipe_server
5      -      RUNNING    2        dwc2_rpi3
6      -      RUNNING    4        network
8      -      RUNNING    5        gpio_rpi3
9      -      RUNNING    1        sd_sdhost_rpi3
10     -      RUNNING    1        read_only_file_system_server
11     -      RUNNING    1        fat_file_system_server
13     -      RUNNING    1        tsh
14     13     RUNNING    1        ps
```

This is what a microkernel looks like from the inside. The serial driver, the USB and SD
card drivers, both filesystems and the network stack are not part of `kernel`; each is a
process of its own, listed here beside the shell.

```
/$ python /hello.py
hello from tailos
```

`python` prints nothing for several seconds before its line. The first run after boot is the
slow one: about 4 seconds on our 4-CPU machine with QEMU 10.2, and about 17 on the 2-CPU
cloud machine with QEMU 8.2. It has not hung. Run it again and it takes under a second on
our machine and about 4 seconds on the cloud machine.

```
/$ ping -c 3 10.0.2.2
PING 10.0.2.2 (10.0.2.2)
reply from 10.0.2.2: seq=0 time=7.199 ms
reply from 10.0.2.2: seq=1 time=3.441 ms
reply from 10.0.2.2: seq=2 time=2.982 ms
--- 10.0.2.2 statistics ---
3 sent, 3 received, 0% lost
```

`10.0.2.2` is QEMU's gateway on the emulated network. The replies travel through the
guest's USB network device, its driver and the `network` process above. The times differ
on every run. With 2 CPUs a reply can miss ping's 1-second timeout: that probe prints
`no reply: seq=N`, and the last line counts it as lost.

If you would rather not run a script, the same steps by hand. Run them in an empty
directory: they keep no cache, the files land there, `gunzip` stops and asks before
replacing files an earlier run left behind, and it unpacks the disk image to 256 MiB.

```bash
mkdir tailos-manual && cd tailos-manual
curl -fsSLO https://tail-os.com/downloads/tail_qemu.rfs.gz
curl -fsSLO https://tail-os.com/downloads/tail_disk.img.gz
curl -fsSLO https://tail-os.com/downloads/SHA256SUMS
gunzip tail_qemu.rfs.gz tail_disk.img.gz
sha256sum -c --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS

qemu-system-aarch64 \
    -M raspi3b \
    -kernel tail_qemu.rfs \
    -serial mon:stdio \
    -display none \
    -drive file=tail_disk.img,format=raw,if=sd \
    -netdev user,id=tailnet0 \
    -device usb-net,netdev=tailnet0
```

`-M raspi3b` emulates a Raspberry Pi 3B. The last two flags give the guest a USB network
device behind QEMU's user-mode networking, which needs no special permissions on your
machine; without them the guest boots with no network.

- [Periodic framework — Rust](../framework/periodic/doc/periodic_framework_public.md):
  write a node that runs on a fixed period.
- [Periodic framework — Python](../framework/periodic/doc/periodic_python_public.md):
  the same, in Python.

The SDK is what you build TAIL OS applications with: the portable OS and the
toolchain that targets it. It needs no TAIL OS source and no cross-compiler —
the bundled toolchain links with its own `rust-lld`.

TAIL OS ships as two artifacts. The SDK here is **board-agnostic**: install it
once and the same install serves every board. A **bootable image** for a
specific board is built from a separate per-board BSP against this SDK. The
Raspberry Pi 3 BSP is a download too: see
[Installing TAIL OS on Raspberry Pi 3](install_rpi3.md).

To try TAIL OS without installing anything, see the [Quick Start](quick_start_public.md):
it boots a prebuilt image in QEMU with one script.

| | |
|---|---|
| Linux on x86-64 | The bundled toolchain runs there |
| `rustup` | The installer registers the bundled toolchain with it: [rustup.rs](https://rustup.rs) |
| `curl` and `tar` | Usually preinstalled |

QEMU is needed only to boot an image, not to build applications:
`sudo apt-get install -y qemu-system-arm qemu-utils`.

```bash
curl -O https://tail-os.com/downloads/tail-sdk-installer-0.1.0.tar.gz
curl -O https://tail-os.com/downloads/SHA256SUMS
sha256sum -c --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS
```

The bundle is 289 MiB: it carries the toolchain and the portable OS, so nothing
is fetched during installation.

```bash
tar xzf tail-sdk-installer-0.1.0.tar.gz
cd tail-sdk-installer-0.1.0
./install.sh --prefix ~/tail-sdk
```

`install.sh` copies the toolchain and the portable OS into the directory you
name, registers the toolchain with rustup as `tail_release` pointing there, and
writes `~/tail-sdk/tail-sdk-env.sh`, which exports `TAIL_SDK` (the SDK tree
inside the install, `~/tail-sdk/sdk/tail-sdk-0.1.0`). It finishes by
compiling and linking a throwaway program, so a successful run means the next
step works. The extracted bundle is disposable afterwards.

Run it without `--prefix` to be prompted for the directory, with `--profile` to
add the env file to your shell startup, and with `--force` to reinstall over an
existing install.

```bash
cargo +tail_release new my_app && cd my_app
cargo +tail_release build --target aarch64-unknown-tail
```

That produces an AArch64 ELF for TAIL OS with no further configuration. The
`+tail_release` selects the installed toolchain; `rustup default tail_release`
makes a bare `cargo build` use it.

Application builds need nothing else. `TAIL_SDK` matters only when building a
board BSP, whose `verify-sdk.sh` reads it:

```bash
source ~/tail-sdk/tail-sdk-env.sh
```

- [Installing TAIL OS on Raspberry Pi 3](install_rpi3.md): download the BSP,
  `bsp-rpi3.zip`, and build an SD card image against this SDK. Programs that use
  the periodic framework are built there too.
- [The periodic framework in Rust](../framework/periodic/doc/periodic_framework_public.md)
  and [in Python](../framework/periodic/doc/periodic_python_public.md): the API
  for periodic applications, with examples.
- [Quick Start](quick_start_public.md): boot a prebuilt image in QEMU.
- [Running TAIL OS in QEMU](install_qemu.md).

chunks.docTitle: Robot Applications on TAIL OS: Concepts
chunks.text:
TailOS is a microkernel real-time operating system for robots. User programs get the full
Rust standard library, and Python runs on the same framework. A robot application is a set
of small programs: **nodes** that run on a fixed period and exchange data on **topics**,
and **services** that answer requests. This page names the pieces and shows where each
one runs. The guides linked at the end show how to write them.

chunks.docTitle: Robot Applications on TAIL OS: Concepts
chunks.text:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
  accTitle: What runs where in a TailOS robot application
  accDescr: Periodic nodes, aperiodic services, device drivers, servers and shell tools are each separate user-space processes. Nodes reach the microkernel through topics and services through requests; the drivers, servers and tools also run on the microkernel, which provides threads, scheduling, memory, IPC and topics.
  NODE["periodic nodes: sensor, estimator, controller"]
  SVC["aperiodic services: request and reply"]
  DRV["device drivers: GPIO, I2C, PWM, stepper"]
  SRV["servers: file system, terminal, log"]
  TOOLS["shell tools: topic, node, param, logview"]
  KERNEL["microkernel: threads, scheduling, memory, IPC, topics"]
  NODE -->|"topics"| KERNEL
  SVC -->|"requests"| KERNEL
  DRV --> KERNEL
  SRV --> KERNEL
  TOOLS --> KERNEL
```

*Your nodes and services, the drivers, the servers and the tools are all separate
user-space processes; the microkernel underneath provides only threads, scheduling, memory,
IPC and topics.*

The kernel does as little as it can: it creates processes and threads, schedules them by
priority, isolates their memory, and carries messages between them. Everything else runs
as an ordinary process with its own address space, so a fault in a driver or a server
cannot corrupt the kernel or another program.

chunks.docTitle: Robot Applications on TAIL OS: Concepts
chunks.text:
| | Periodic node | Aperiodic service |
|---|---|---|
| Runs | once per declared period: wake, read inputs, compute, publish | once per request: receive, handle, reply exactly once |
| Talks over | topics: many readers, the latest value | requests: one client, one reply |
| You write | one function with a `#[periodic]` attribute | a trait, its implementation, and a client call |
| Typical use | sensor drivers, estimators, controllers, actuator commands | device drivers, configuration, anything asked for on demand |

A **periodic node** is the shape most robot code takes. You declare its period, what it
does on an overrun, and what it reads and publishes; the framework owns the loop:

```rust
#[periodic(every = "20ms", on_overrun = Skip)]
fn brake(
    #[subscribe(SENSOR_RANGE, stale_after = "70ms")] range: Cycle<Range>,
    #[publish(CMD_VELOCITY)] command: Out<Twist>,
) {
    command.publish(match range.get() {
        Some(reading) if reading.range > 0.30 => cruise(),
        _ => stop(),   // too close, no reading, or a reading too old
    });
}
```

What the framework does for every node:

- **Fixed timing.** Each release wakes at an absolute time on the period's grid, so the
  period never drifts. An overrun is detected, handled by the declared policy, and
  reported.
- **Freshness.** Each input has a `stale_after` bound. A reading that never arrived and a
  reading that is too old are the same case, `None`, so a node cannot act on stale data
  by accident.
- **All-or-nothing outputs.** What the body publishes goes out when the body returns, in
  declaration order. A body that panics halfway publishes nothing.

An **aperiodic service** is a server: a client calls it and blocks until the one reply
arrives. Drivers are services, and so is anything an application asks for on demand.

chunks.docTitle: Robot Applications on TAIL OS: Concepts
chunks.text:
A topic is a named stream of fixed-size values, with any number of readers. Each reader
gets the latest value; a slow reader misses values but never blocks the writer. A topic is
defined once, in a crate both ends import, with its name, its payload type and its
**lane**:

```rust
pub const SENSOR_RANGE: Topic<Range, SafeLane>   = Topic::new("sensor/range");
pub const CMD_VELOCITY: Topic<Twist, KernelLane> = Topic::new("cmd/velocity");
```

| Lane | How a value travels | Safety class |
|---|---|---|
| `KernelLane` | copied in and out by the kernel, one system call per message; payloads up to 4 KiB | safety |
| `SafeLane` | zero-copy through shared memory; the kernel lets the writer change only the slot it is filling, so a published value cannot be corrupted | safety |
| `FastLane` | zero-copy through shared memory, no system call per message, no such protection | quality-managed |

Changing a topic's lane is a one-word edit to its definition; no node changes. A node
declared `safety` refuses to build if it reads or publishes a topic on a quality-managed
lane.

Both ends of a topic must agree on the payload. Every payload type has a **layout
identity** computed from its fields, and an end whose payload differs in size or layout
is refused when it opens the topic, with a message that says why.

chunks.docTitle: Robot Applications on TAIL OS: Concepts
chunks.text:
- **Standard payloads** (`robot_messages`): `Vector3`, `Point`, `Quaternion`, `Pose`,
  `Twist`, `Range`, `Imu`, `Odometry`, in SI units; sensor and odometry records carry a
  time stamp in nanoseconds since boot.
  Rust and Python read the same definitions, and the Python module is generated from the
  Rust structs by the build.
- **Your own payloads** are plain structs that derive `WirePlain`, which proves at build
  time that they have no padding and computes their layout identity.
- **Coordinate frames** (`frames`): a robot's frames are declared once as a tree, checked
  at build time, and looked up with `lookup(target, source)`, with no allocation and a
  bounded cost. A moving link takes its value from a node input, so it goes stale like any
  other input.

chunks.docTitle: Robot Applications on TAIL OS: Concepts
chunks.text:
| Feature | What you get |
|---|---|
| Run-time parameters | declare a gain with a default and a range; change it from the shell with `param set` while the node runs |
| Actions | a long-running goal (drive to a point, home an axis) with feedback, cancel and a dead-man lease |
| Release journal | every node with an output journals each release, so a recording can replay it |
| Description | every node announces its period, inputs, outputs and parameters, which `node info` prints |

chunks.docTitle: Robot Applications on TAIL OS: Concepts
chunks.text:
```text
tsh> topic record -o /recordings/run7.mcap &     record every topic
tsh> lidar & brake & drive &                     run the robot
tsh> brake --replay /recordings/run7.mcap        re-run one node against what it saw
replay: brake life 1: 2104 releases, 2103 compared, identical
```

Recordings are standard MCAP files. Replaying a node runs its body once per recorded
release, with exactly the inputs, parameters and timing that release had, and compares
every output. An edited node replays too, which answers "what would it have done?".

chunks.docTitle: Robot Applications on TAIL OS: Concepts
chunks.text:
| | Rust | Python |
|---|---|---|
| Periodic nodes | `#[periodic]` attribute | `@periodic` decorator |
| Parameters, actions, record and replay | yes | yes |
| Coordinate frames | yes | not yet |
| Services and device classes | yes | no |

A Rust node and a Python node exchange topics with each other; both use the same
transports.

chunks.docTitle: Robot Applications on TAIL OS: Concepts
chunks.text:
- TailOS targets the Raspberry Pi 3. The robotics framework is tested on the QEMU
  emulation of that board. The Python interpreter is not yet on the board image.
- No process supervisor ships: a node that exits is not restarted.
- Run-time parameter values last for the node's life; a restart starts at the defaults.

chunks.docTitle: Robot Applications on TAIL OS: Concepts
chunks.text:
- [Periodic nodes in Rust](../framework/periodic/doc/periodic_framework_public.md)
- [Periodic nodes in Python](../framework/periodic/doc/periodic_python_public.md)
- [Services in Rust](../framework/aperiodic/doc/aperiodic_framework_public.md)
- [Devices in Rust](../framework/device/doc/device_framework_public.md)
- [Shell tools](../utility/doc/shell_tools_public.md)

Declare a period and the topics; the framework owns the timing loop, topic admission,
freshness and the publish. A node is a function with an attribute — there is no `main` to
write.

A **periodic node** is what you would otherwise create by hand as a thread running a timer
loop — spawn a task, read the clock, do the work, sleep for the remainder, repeat. The
framework replaces that loop, so you never write the thread, the sleep, or the drift
correction the hand-written version needs.

A node reads any number of topics, each declared on the parameter that receives it and each
with its own freshness bound, and publishes any number, each declared on the parameter that
hands the body its output.

For why the framework works this way, see the
[design document](periodic_framework_design.md). This page is the Rust API. The
[C](periodic_c_public.md) and [Python](periodic_python_public.md) pages describe theirs;
their move to the grammar on this page follows in the next change on this branch and is
not yet verified.

Four files in the BSP's `app/` directory: the topics, defined once, and three programs that each have an end of one. No program writes a `main`, a thread, a sleep or a retry loop. | File | Is | |---|---| | `app/robot_topics.rs` | the topics: each one's name, payload and lane | | `app/lidar/src/main.rs` | a node that publishes `sensor/range` | | `app/brake/src/main.rs` | a node that reads `sensor/range` | | `app/drive/src/main.rs` | a node that reads `sensor/range` and `cmd/velocity` | ```mermaid flowchart LR lidar["lidar
every 20 ms"] -- "sensor/range
SafeLane" --> brake["brake
every 20 ms"] lidar -- "sensor/range" --> drive["drive
every 20 ms"] pad["a pad, a planner
(not written here)"] -- "cmd/velocity
KernelLane" --> drive ```

Each program is built with the Raspberry Pi 3 board support package (BSP). Add
`/usr/bin/lidar=lidar`, and the same line for `brake` and `drive`, to the `[disk]` section
of the BSP's `tail.build`; `./make-disk.sh` builds each `app/<name>/src/main.rs` against
the SDK's `periodic` crate and puts it in `/usr/bin` on the image. There is no
`Cargo.toml` to write. See
[Installing TAIL OS on Raspberry Pi 3](../../../doc/install_rpi3.md#add-your-own-programs).
A program's name is at most 32 bytes: a longer one is left out of the image's program
table, so it never starts and leaves no record (TAIL-501).

On the booted image start them in the background, in any order: `lidar &`, `brake &`,
`drive &`. No program names another. The framework opens each topic and waits for its
publisher (see [Start-up](#start-up)). Nothing here publishes `cmd/velocity`, so `drive`
runs and stays stopped: that input is absent, and absent is the `_` arm.

`periodic`, `wire_plain` and `robot_messages` are libraries of the SDK, so a program names
each with a `use` and nothing more. Two lines are there only because the BSP's one-file
programs share a file:

| Line | Why |
|---|---|
| `#[path = "../../robot_topics.rs"] mod robot_topics;` | compiles the one definitions file into this program |
| `#![allow(dead_code)]`, in the definitions file | a program that leaves a definition unused would otherwise be warned about it |

**In a cargo workspace the definitions are a library crate instead**, which is how the
tree's own nodes are built (`test/integration_test/tests/periodic_test_topics`, and the
nodes beside it). `robot_topics/src/lib.rs` then needs no `#![allow(dead_code)]`; each
program lists `periodic` and `robot_topics` in its `Cargo.toml` and starts at its `use`
lines. A payload that a C or Python program must also read lives in a crate of its own that
depends on `wire_plain` alone, as `test/integration_test/tests/periodic_test_payloads`
does: the host generator that prints its C and Python definitions imports it, and cannot
import a crate that depends on `periodic`. The rest of this page shows a program from its
`use` lines on.

Where the examples come from:

| Example | Is |
|---|---|
| the quick start: `robot_topics.rs`, `lidar`, `brake` and the two-input `drive`, verbatim | the compile-pass fixture `test/unit_test/compile_pass/periodic_quick_start`, which keeps them in the BSP's `app/` layout, built on the host by `make ci-compile-pass` |
| the balancing robot's own payload under [Payloads](#payloads) | the compile-pass fixture `test/unit_test/compile_pass/periodic_own_payload_without_unsafe`, built with `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` |
| the two-input `drive` of [Several inputs](#several-inputs), `monitor`, `estimator`, `clearance`, the state between two inputs, the state taken as `&u32`, `echo`, the migrated `overrun_pipe` | a compile-pass fixture under `test/unit_test/compile_pass/periodic_*`, built on the host by `make ci-compile-pass` |
| the three-input `drive` | the node program `drive` of `test/unit_test/periodic_macro_test`, run on the host |
| `lidar`, `counter` | the on-target nodes `periodic_framework_node` (its function named `pilot`, so its journal is `pilot/__releases` beside the quick start's `lidar`) and `periodic_framework_stateful_node` under `test/integration_test/tests`, run on QEMU raspi3b |
| the refused declarations: the table under [What the build refuses](#what-the-build-refuses), the `safety` node on `DEBUG_SCAN`, the node before its migration | a fixture under `test/unit_test/compile_fail/periodic_*`, refused on the host by `make ci-compile-fail` |
| `brake`, `teleop`, `filter`, `nearest`, `odometer`, the publisher on some releases, the `Fault` publisher, the two-output `drive` of [Several outputs](#several-outputs), the lidar with a second output and the stand of [Raw ends](#raw-ends), the `parse_duration` program | a variation of those, written for this page; no build in the tree compiles it |

Each is shown with its topics imported from `robot_topics` instead of written beside the
node, and a fixture's payloads with the fields `robot_topics` gives them.

The header says what is true of the node. A topic the node reads is declared on the
parameter that receives it, and a topic it publishes on the parameter that publishes it.

| Where | Key | Required |
|---|---|---|
| header | `every = "<duration>"` | always |
| header | `on_overrun = Skip \| CatchUp \| Fault` | always |
| header | `init = <expr>` | exactly when the body takes a state |
| header | `safety` | no |
| parameter | `#[subscribe(TOPIC, stale_after = "<duration>")]` | once per input |
| parameter | `#[publish(TOPIC)]` | once per output |

```rust
#[periodic(every = "20ms", on_overrun = Skip)]
```

The release period. Releases fall on `start + n * period`, never drifting. A
[duration](#durations).

```rust
#[periodic(every = "20ms", on_overrun = Skip)]
```

What to do when a cycle runs past its next release: `Skip`, `CatchUp`, or `Fault`, written
as the bare word. No default — omitting it does not compile. See
[`OverrunPolicy`](#overrunpolicy).

```rust
use periodic::{periodic, Out};
use robot_topics::{Range, SENSOR_RANGE};

#[periodic(every = "20ms", on_overrun = Skip)]
fn lidar(#[publish(SENSOR_RANGE)] range: Out<Range>) {
    range.publish(Range { stamp_ns: periodic::monotonic_ns(), range: 4.2, ..Range::default() });
}
```

One output: the topic the body publishes on. The parameter's type is `Out<T>` of the
topic's payload, `periodic::Out<'_, T>` with its lifetime left out. The body hands it a
whole value with `publish`, which takes the handle, so an output publishes at most once a
release. Nothing is sent at the call: every value handed to an output is published when
the body ends, in the order the outputs are declared, and nothing at all is published for
a body that panics. A node has as many outputs as it has such parameters, each on its own
topic. An output the body does not publish on a release publishes nothing on that release
(see [Publishing on some releases](#publishing-on-some-releases)).

A node returns nothing: the output is the parameter, never the return value.

```rust
#[periodic(every = "20ms", on_overrun = Skip)]
fn brake(#[subscribe(SENSOR_RANGE, stale_after = "70ms")] lidar: Cycle<Range>) {
    brake_for(lidar.get().map_or(0.0, |reading| reading.range));
}
```

One input: the topic, then how old a reading may be before it reads as absent to this

Age is measured from **receipt at this node**, on the clock the cadence runs on. A reading
the body acts on was received no more than `stale_after` ago, and so was published no
earlier than `stale_after` plus the previous sampling gap ago. That gap is one period in
steady state.

Limits:

- **After a late wake-up the gap is the whole delay, and that release is not told so**
  (TAIL-487). The drive node (every 20 ms, command bound `"310ms"`) is kept off the
  processor for one second, during which its planner publishes a last command and dies.
  The first release after the stall is handed that command as received now —
  `since_received()` is zero, `arrived()` is true, `overruns()` is zero — and the node
  drives on it for 310 ms more. The releases it missed are reported by `overruns()` on the
  release after.
- **A bound shorter than the node's period is accepted.** `every = "20ms"` with
  `stale_after = "5ms"` and a 40 ms publisher: the input is usable on the release a
  publication arrives and stale on the next, for ever.
- **Nothing checks the sizing rule below.**

```
stale_after >= (lost publications tolerated + 1) x the publisher's period + this node's period
```

and never a multiple of this node's period: write it half a period off.

The age a node observes is a whole number of its own periods, give or take wake-up
jitter, so a bound on a multiple is decided by microseconds. `"60ms"` on a 20 ms node: a
reading received at one release is 60 ms old three releases later, a few microseconds
more or less, and whether it is still usable there depends on which of the two wake-ups
ran later. `"70ms"` decides it 10 ms clear of any release.

| Input | Publisher | Tolerates | Rule | Written |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `range` of the 20 ms drive node | every 20 ms | 1 lost | `2 x 20 + 20 = 60` | `"70ms"` |
| `permit` of the 20 ms drive node | every 50 ms | 1 lost | `2 x 50 + 20 = 120` | `"130ms"` |

A node reacts at a release, so it drops an input between `stale_after` and
`stale_after` plus two periods after the publisher's last publication, scheduling delay

A value you tune while the node runs -- a gain, a limit, a flag -- is a run-time parameter.
Declare it on the argument that receives it, with its default and its range:

```rust
#[periodic(every = "5ms", on_overrun = Skip)]
fn balance(
    #[subscribe(IMU, stale_after = "12ms")] imu: Cycle<Imu>,
    #[param(default = 42.0, range = 0.0..=200.0)] kp: f32,
    #[param(default = 1.5, range = 0.0..=20.0)] kd: f32,
    #[publish(MOTOR_COMMAND)] command: Out<MotorCommand>,
) {
    command.publish(match imu.get() {
        Some(imu) => MotorCommand::torque(kp * imu.pitch + kd * imu.pitch_rate),
        None => MotorCommand::STOP,
    });
}
```

- The argument's name is the parameter's name, at most 23 bytes; its type is one of `bool`,
  `i32`, `i64`, `u32`, `u64`, `f32`, `f64`, written as the type itself. `range` names both
  ends and includes them, and is required for every kind but `bool`, which takes none:
  `#[param(default = false)] armed: bool`. The default and the bounds may be named
  constants, and are checked when the node is built. At most 16 parameters per node.
- The body is handed each value by value, on every release; reading one costs nothing.

From the shell, with `param`:

```text
tsh> param list balance
kp = 42.0  (0.0 .. 200.0)
kd = 1.5   (0.0 .. 20.0)
tsh> param set balance kp 45.5
balance: kp = 45.5 from release 18342
tsh> param list balance
kp = 45.5  (0.0 .. 200.0, default 42.0)
kd = 1.5   (0.0 .. 20.0)
tsh> param set balance kp 250
param: balance kp = 250.0 is outside 0.0 .. 200.0; nothing was set
tsh> param list
balance  2 parameters
```

- **A set takes effect at the start of a release.** The release `param set` names is the
  first whose body is handed the new value; a body never sees a value change while it
  runs. `param set` reports success only on the node's own answer, and exits 1 with what
  was refused, or when the node does not answer within eight of its periods and 250 ms.
- **Set coupled gains in one command.** `param set balance kp 50 kd 2.5` is one request,
  applied whole at one release. Two commands are two requests, and at least one release
  between them runs with the new `kp` and the old `kd`.
- **The node checks every request**, against its declared range, exactly, both ends
  included: a value outside it, a NaN, or a name it does not declare is refused and
  nothing changes, whoever sent it. `param` refuses the same way before it sends.
- **Values live for the node's life.** A restart or a reboot starts at the defaults again.
  To keep a value, change its default in the source; `param list` shows each changed value
  beside its default, so what to copy is on the screen.
- **A node declared `safety` declares no parameter.** Its configuration is part of its
  verified build: `#[param]` on it fails the build, and the fix is a `const`.
- **Each applied change is in the system log**, written by `param` into its own ring,
  `balance: kp 42.0 -> 45.5 from release 18342` (`logview -s param`). A change made by a
  program that writes the request topic itself is in the node's state and its journal, not
  in the log.
- **Recorded and replayed.** Every release-journal record carries the values its body was
  handed, so a replay hands each body the values it ran with, and a recording across sets
  replays `identical`. Renaming, retyping, adding, removing or reordering a parameter is a
  new declaration, which replay refuses; a changed default or range replays.
- **Every running node is listed by `node`**, whatever it declares; `param list` names only
  the nodes that declare parameters. `node info` says whether a node's parameters can be
  set (pids illustrative):

```text
tsh> node list
balance  pid 7  balance
tsh> node info balance
balance
  Process: pid 7 (balance), thread 0
  Period: 5ms, on_overrun Skip
  Priority: 31
  Subscribers:
    imu/data: safe, stale_after 12ms
  Publishers:
    motor/command: kernel
  Action Servers:
  Parameters: 2, settable
```

What it costs and what it takes:

- **One non-blocking read per release**, of the node's request topic, between the sampling
  and the body; almost always it finds nothing. A release that finds a request also checks
  at most 16 values and publishes the node's state. All of it is inside the cycle the
  overrun accounting measures.
- **Two kernel-lane topics per node with parameters**, `<node>/__params` (its state) and
  `<node>/__param_set` (requests): count them in the image's `[topic]` budget, two table
  entries and 2 pages for a node of up to two parameters, 8 at 16.
- When they cannot be opened -- the topic storage is used up, or a recorder still holds the
  topics of a previous life with another table -- the node runs on its defaults, unsettable,
  and says so once, before its first release, at WARNING:

```text
balance: no parameter topics (topic storage full); runs with its defaults
```

- **Run a settable node whose timing matters from the RFS, not from FAT.** Its
  request-handling code is first executed when it handles its first request, and a node
  loaded from FAT faults those pages in from the file system inside that release.
- **Any program can set a parameter**, within its declared range, by writing the request
  topic, as any program can publish any kernel-lane topic today; a value outside the range
  never reaches a body. Writer authorisation for named topics is TAIL-632.

The handle keeps its goal alive while it is polled: a keep-alive goes out once per server
period. A goal whose keep-alives stop -- its client killed, crashed, hung, or simply not
polling -- is stopped by the node when its lease runs out, and ends `Abandoned`.

- **The lease is required**, and must be at least twice the node's period: `lease = "39ms"`
  on a 20 ms node does not start, `could not start: lease 39ms is shorter than twice the
  period 20ms`.
- **Choose about five periods**: `lease = "100ms"` on a 20 ms node. That rides out a lost
  keep-alive and a client a period late, and a client node up to four periods slow.
- **A killed client's goal stops within the lease and two periods**: at 20 ms and 100 ms,
  about 140 ms after the client's last keep-alive, plus the releases' lateness. There is no
  death signal to stop it sooner; the lease covers a killed, a hung and a starved client
  alike.
- **A periodic client slower than the lease loses every goal.** A client node polls once per
  its own release, so its keep-alives are its period apart: a client at 150 ms against a
  100 ms lease sees each goal end `Abandoned`. Give the server a lease longer than the
  slowest client's period and one server period.
- **A program that stops polling loses its goal too**: `let drive = DRIVE_TO.send(goal)?;
  long_work(); drive.wait()` is abandoned during `long_work`. Poll, or call `feedback` or
  `wait`, while the goal should run.

chunks.text:
- **One non-blocking read per release** of the action's request topic, almost always finding
  nothing, and one status publish of at most 4096 bytes, both inside the cycle the overrun
  accounting measures. Nothing is allocated and nothing is logged.
- **Two kernel-lane topics per action**, `<action>/__goal` and `<action>/__status`: count them
  in the image's `[topic]` budget, two table entries and the pages of a goal record (24
  bytes and the goal) and of a status (176 bytes, the feedback and the result).
- **A serving node whose action topics cannot be opened does not start**, naming the action:
  `drive: could not start: action drive_to: drive_to/__goal: topic storage full`.
- **Recorded and replayed.** Every release-journal record carries the goal its body was
  handed, so a replay hands each body the goal it ran with and opens no action topic; what
  the body says of it -- feedback, a result -- is not compared, only the node's output is.
- **Any program can send, keep, cancel or replace a goal** by writing the request topic and
  stating another process's id, as any program can publish any kernel-lane topic today. The
  lease and the device's own lease stay the stop.

Every node with an output publishes, on every release, one record on a kernel-lane topic of
its own, `<node>/__releases`, where `<node>` is the node function's name: `lidar` publishes
`lidar/__releases`. The author writes nothing for it, and nothing turns it off. A node with
no output publishes none.

```text
 release k:  sleep -> read the clock -> sample the inputs -> publish record k -> body
             -> publish each output, in declaration order
 record k:   k, the clock reading, the overruns delivered, what became of each of release
             k-1's outputs (two bits each: none, declined, published, refused);
             the process that published it;
             per input: arrived, missed, rejected, and the reading if it arrived (zeros if not);
             the values of its run-time parameters, which release k's body is handed;
             release k-1's outputs, end to end in declaration order (zeros for one the body
             did not publish)
```

It is what a recording of the run (`topic record`) needs to replay a node exactly. The
record of release k is published **before** the body runs, so a body that panics or hangs
leaves the release it ran on behind. Its payload is `32 + M` bytes, `M` the inputs' facts
and payloads, 8 bytes per run-time parameter and the outputs' payloads, all rounded up to 8,
and at most the kernel lane's 4096 B; its layout identity is the node's declaration
identity, over the period, the overrun policy, each input's payload type, each parameter's
name and kind, and each output's payload type, in order. A node with more than 16 outputs,
or whose record would pass 4096 B, runs without a journal and logs a WARNING saying why. `topic list`
shows it as `layout 0x…`.

What it costs and what it takes:

- **One kernel-lane publish per release**, of at most 4096 B, between the sampling and the
  body. It never waits on a reader, and it is inside the cycle the overrun accounting
  measures: a journal that made a release late is reported as an overrun.
- **One topic per node with an output, in the image's topic budget**: one table entry and
  the record's pages (one page for a record up to 192 B, two up to 384 B, five at 1 KiB, 20
  at 4 KiB). Count it when you size `[topic]` in `tail.build`.
- **4 KiB of stack in every node with an output**, journal or not: the buffer each record
  is built in, held for the node's life beside its inputs' readings.

When it cannot be opened -- the topic storage is used up, the record would exceed 4096 B,
or the topic is held with another declaration's shape -- the node runs exactly as it would
with one, and says so once, before its first release, at WARNING:


**A node's name must be unique within an image.** Two node functions of the same name
share one journal topic: a second one of another declaration finds the topic held with
another shape, takes that refusal, and runs without a journal. The same program started
twice shares one journal too, and its records interleave; each names its process, and a
replay refuses them.

C and Python nodes run their own loop and journal through the same record: their pages say
how ([C](periodic_c_public.md#recording-and-replay),
[Python](periodic_python_public.md#recording-and-replay)).

Record a run, then run one node of it again, offline, against exactly what it saw:

```text
tsh> topic record -o /recordings/run7.mcap &        FIRST: before the nodes
tsh> lidar & brake & drive &
     ... the run ...
tsh> brake --replay /recordings/run7.mcap
replay: brake life 1: 2104 releases, 2103 compared, identical
facts: sensor/range: 5 releases without an arrival, 3 missed, 0 rejected; cmd/velocity: 0, 0, 0; 1 overruns
replay: running release 2103, the life's last; its output is in no record
```

`--replay FILE` goes **at the end** of the node's own command line, with `--life N` after it
to pick a later life of the node (a restart during the recording is life 2). Nothing in the
node changes: the journal above is what replay reads, and the generated `main` reads the two
options. Replay runs the node's `init` and then its body once per recorded release, handing
each input exactly the reading, the loss counts and the overruns that release was handed,
and each run-time parameter the value it was handed, at the recorded clock reading. It opens no topic, publishes nothing and never sleeps, and it
compares what the body hands each output with what the node published there, release by
release; a difference names the output by its topic:

```text
replay: brake life 1: first divergence at release 2059:
  output cmd/brake byte 0: recorded 00 00 00 00, replayed 9a 99 19 3e
replay: 1 of 2103 compared releases differ
```

exit 1. What it recomputes with the binary you run are every input's age and staleness and
the body, so an edited body or a changed `stale_after` is a what-if: "would brake have
stopped earlier with `stale_after = "40ms"`?" An input or output of another type, another
order, period or policy, or a parameter of another name, kind or order, is refused, naming
both declarations; a changed default or range replays.

- **Start `topic record` before the nodes.** A node's journal is whole from its first
  release only when the recorder is already running; otherwise the replay is refused:
  `life 1 starts at release 37: the recorder attached after brake started`. A node faster
  than every 15 ms can lose its first records even so.
- **The last release runs uncompared.** Its output is in no record: the node was stopped,
  crashed, or the recording ended. Replay says its verdict first, then runs it -- so a body
  that crashed in the recording crashes the same way in the replay, which is the point.
- **Replay runs `init` and the body as written.** A node that opens a device or calls a
  driver does so in a replay too: replay such a node only where the device is absent, or
  replay the nodes downstream of it, whose inputs are its recorded output.
- **What replay cannot see** shows up as a divergence, never as a false `identical`: time
  read other than through `periodic::now()` or a `Cycle`, side effects other than the outputs,
  the node's own command-line arguments (give the same ones), anything depending on
  `HashMap` order.
- **A node with no output cannot be replayed**: there is nothing to compare, and it is
  refused before its `init` runs. Neither can one whose journal the recorder lost: a lost
  stretch is replayed up to, and the rest is not claimed.

Refusals are on standard error and exit 1 (a malformed `--replay ...` tail exits 2); the
verdict is on standard output.

An application writes no retry loop and no start-up ordering. - **The outputs first, in the order written**, so two nodes that read each other both start: each creates its topics before it waits for the other's. - **A served action after the inputs**, its goal reader before its status writer, so a client, which sends only once it has read a status, never sends to a reader that does not exist yet. A refusal fails the start, naming the action: serving it is what the node is declared for (see [Actions](#actions)). - **The release journal, and then the node's description, last**: the journal for a node with an output (see [The release journal](#the-release-journal)), the description `/__node`, which `node list` reads, for every node. Opened after everything the node declares, neither ever takes a table entry one of the node's own topics needs, and neither, refused, stops the node. - **One budget for the whole node**: 2 000 "nobody publishes this yet" answers, 5 ms apart. Ten seconds, whatever the number of inputs. Only that answer is waited on; any other refusal ends the start at once. - **Nothing published before the node starts reaches it.** What each input collected during admission is dropped, and loss from before the start is not reported. - **A node does not run until every topic it declares is open.** The drive node with no
  `lidar`: ten seconds, one ERROR record, exit status 1, and its body never ran. What
  tells the rest of a system that a node is not running is silence on the topic it
  publishes.
- **A kernel-lane input never fails the start for absence.** Subscribing creates the
  topic, so a kernel-lane topic nobody publishes, or one whose name is misspelt, is not a
  start-up failure: the node starts and that input is absent for ever. The topic its open
  created goes with it when the node ends.
- **A kernel-lane input opened early holds nothing while the node waits.** It is opened in
  the order written, so it may wait ten seconds for a later input's publisher. The topic
  keeps what is published meanwhile, and the start drops it in one read.
- **Only the first missing topic is named.** Three safe-lane publishers down: three
  ten-second runs to learn all three.
- **An output created before a failed start stays without a writer.** A downstream
  node is admitted against it and receives nothing. The failed node names it, one record per
  output created. On `KernelLane` the topic goes with its last end, so once no reader holds it, a
  restarted node can create it again.
- **A publication that lands between an input's drop and the first release's sampling is
  handed over at release 0.** What holds at release 0 is that nothing published before
  the start is shown. Beside a publisher that is running, an input can show a reading
  there.
- **A topic published once, or only when its value changes, cannot be an input.** A node
  that starts after the publication never receives it.
- **A mistyped duration is a start-up failure, not a build failure** (TAIL-485). See

A topic's lane is part of its type, written once, in its definition. A node names no
lane, and the inputs of one node may be on different lanes. Changing a topic's lane is a
change to that one line, and every end follows.

| Lane | Copies | Kernel calls per message | Writers | May carry data a safety requirement depends on | Holds for a reader |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `KernelLane` | one in, into the topic's own slots in the kernel, and one out to each reader; payload at most 4 KiB | one to publish, one to read | **up to 4 at once** | yes | the latest value; the topic also keeps its newest 8 publications, and up to 20 |
| `SafeLane` | none | four | **exactly one** | yes: the writer cannot alter a frame a reader is inside | the latest value |
| `FastLane` | none | none | **exactly one** | **no — Quality Managed only** | the latest value |

Choose the one with the least machinery that meets the requirement:

| The topic | Lane |
|---|---|
| has more than one writer | `KernelLane`, the only lane that allows it |
| carries a small payload | `KernelLane` |
| carries a large payload, and a reader has a safety requirement | `SafeLane` |
| carries a large payload, and nothing downstream is safety-rated | `FastLane` |

Zero-copy is not "the fast one, always". For a small payload the copy costs less than
establishing a shared region; `tail_core`'s own guidance puts the crossover at roughly
2 KB (`library/tail_core/src/topic/publisher.rs:95` (superseded, at `47d11b68e`); now
`kernel/src/ipc/safe_zero_copy_topic/doc/why_not_kernel_zero_copy.md:99`), and this change
measured neither side of it. The kernel lane carries nothing above 4 KiB: a typed end over
it does not compile.

`FastLane` is Quality Managed by its own design: its writer holds a standing read-write

**`safety` checks the topics a node declares: its inputs and its outputs.** A `safety`
node that declares one on `FastLane` does not build, and the error is at that topic.
Limits:

- **An end a node opens itself is not checked.** A `safety` node that opens
  `periodic::subscriber(&DEBUG_SCAN)` in `init` and reads it in its body builds with no
  error, and its decision rests on a fast-lane topic. So does one that opens a transport
  directly.
- **Under `cargo check` only the attribute's refusal shows.** A call of the library's
  entry point written by hand, without the attribute, is refused too, but only by a full
  build.

**Two ends opened through one definition cannot disagree on the lane or the payload.** That
reaches exactly as far as the shared definition does:

- **Two definitions of one name.** One program writes `Topic<Twist, KernelLane>` and
  another `Topic<Twist, SafeLane>`, both for `"cmd/velocity"`: the kernel-lane subscriber
  starts at once and receives nothing, with no error anywhere (TAIL-489).
- **Across languages.** A C or Python topic is a separately written definition by
  construction, so the same silence is possible there.
- **Two definitions of one name over two payloads that differ.** Caught on every lane,
  whether the two differ in size or only in layout -- a field renamed, retyped or moved,
  a named value renumbered: every lane refuses the second end at open, so its node does
  not start, and the record says what the topic carries (see [Payloads](#payloads)). Two payloads with one
  layout under two names (`Point` and `Vector3`) are one payload to every lane.

|---|---|---|
| `ns` | nanoseconds | `"250ns"` |
| `us` | microseconds | `"500us"` |
| `ms` | milliseconds | `"20ms"` |
| `s` | seconds | `"1s"` |

**Use a standard payload** when one fits: `robot_messages` has `geometry::{Vector3, Point,
Quaternion, Pose, Twist}`, `sensor::{Range, Imu}` and `navigation::Odometry`, with the

SI units in each field's doc comment, and a `stamp_ns` field as the record's time stamp
(nanoseconds since boot: `periodic::monotonic_ns()` at the hardware boundary,
`periodic::now()` in a node that decides, so a replay reproduces it). A C node reads the same payload through `<tail/messages.h>` and a Python node
through `tail_messages`, both generated from these structs by the build.

**Declare your own** as a `#[repr(C)]` struct that derives `WirePlain`:

```rust
use wire_plain::WirePlain;

/// What the balance controller knows at the end of a cycle.
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, Default, PartialEq, WirePlain)]
#[repr(C)]
pub struct BalanceState {
    /// When the cycle ran [ns since boot, monotonic counter].
    pub stamp_ns: u64,
    /// Tilt from upright [rad].
    pub tilt: f32,
    /// Tilt rate [rad/s].
    pub tilt_rate: f32,
    /// Commanded wheel speed [rad/s].
    pub wheel_speed: f32,
    /// Cycles the node has run.
    pub cycle: u32,
}
```

That is the whole of a payload definition, written once, beside the topic's definition,
and imported by both ends. A crate that holds it, its topic and a node builds with
`#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`. A payload crosses shared memory, where another process can
store any bytes, so the derive proves at the definition what that needs:

| The derive requires | Because |
|---|---|
| `#[repr(C)]`, and nothing else in it | both processes, and the generated C and Python, lay the type out the same way |
| named fields of `u8`..`u64`, `i8`..`i64`, `f32`, `f64`, non-empty arrays of them, and other such structs | every bit pattern must be a valid value, of a width every machine and language shares |
| no padding | a gap would carry the sender's uninitialised bytes; name it with a reserved field |
| no type or lifetime parameter (a `const` one is allowed) | whether the struct has padding would depend on the argument |
| field and type names C, C++ and Python can all declare | the C and Python definitions are printed from this struct |

A field's doc comment is part of the payload: its unit is written there, in square
brackets, and reaches the generated C and Python as a comment. An integer field may name
its values: `#[wire_plain(values(ULTRASOUND = 0, INFRARED = 1))]` gives the struct
`Range::ULTRASOUND` and `Range::INFRARED`, typed as the field.

**Two ends must hold one definition, and are checked.** The derive describes the layout,
and its 32-bit identity -- FNV-1a over field names, their order, their types, nesting,
array lengths and named values -- travels with the topic. On every lane an end whose
identity differs is refused at open and its node does not start. The kernel lane also says
what the topic carries:

```
drive: could not start: topic `cmd/velocity` refused the open: this is not the payload type the topic carries: it carries 48-byte payloads of layout 0x38793118
```

That is the record of a node whose `Twist` has `linear` and `angular` exchanged, against a
pad that made the topic with the standard one. The system log keeps 96 bytes of a
`periodic` record, so `logview` shows it cut after "the payload type the", before the
shape; the console and the `NodeError` carry all of it. On the safe and fast lanes the reason ends at "carries". The type's name, the doc
comments and the lane are not compared.

A kernel-lane topic lives while an end holds it, so a corrected definition is not refused
for ever: once every end of the old payload has closed, the corrected one creates the topic
anew.

**The compiler refuses what cannot cross**, at the struct, with the reason:

| Written | Error |
|---|---|
| `{ range: f32, stamp_ns: u64 }` | ``this wire type has padding; a padded value carries the sender's uninitialised bytes across the process boundary. Reorder the fields, or name the gap with an explicit reserved field.`` |
| `pressed: bool` | `` `bool` cannot cross the wire: only 0 and 1 are valid, and a sender may send 2. .. `` |
| `key: char` | `` `char` cannot cross the wire: not every u32 is a valid scalar value. .. `` |
| `frame_id: &'static str`, `*const u8` | `` `a reference` cannot cross the wire: an address is meaningless in another address space. .. `` |
| `handler: fn(u32) -> u32` | `` `a function pointer` cannot cross the wire: the sender would choose where this process jumps. .. `` |
| `count: usize`, `isize` | `` `a pointer-sized integer` cannot cross the wire: its width is the building machine's, .. `` |
| `value: u128`, `i128` | `` `a 128-bit integer` cannot cross the wire: C and Python have no fixed-width type to declare it with. .. `` |
| `id: NonZeroU32` | `` `a niche-optimised type` cannot cross the wire: zero is a valid byte pattern and an invalid value. .. `` |
| the derive on an enum or a union | `` `WirePlain` describes a struct: an enum has bit patterns that are not valid values, and a union has no single layout to read `` |
| no `repr` | `` a wire type declares `#[repr(C)]`: a default Rust layout is whatever the compiler chose for this build, and both sides of the wire must agree forever `` |
| `#[repr(C, packed)]`, `#[repr(C, align(16))]`, `#[repr(transparent)]` | `` a wire type is plain `#[repr(C)]`: `packed`, `align` and `transparent` state a layout the C and Python definitions generated from this struct would not follow `` |
| `struct Metres(pub f32);`, `struct Ping;` | `a wire type names its fields: C and Python read a field by its name, and a tuple or unit struct has none to give them` |
| `struct Nothing {}` | `a wire type has at least one field: zero bytes give the two ends nothing to agree on` |
| `align: [u64; 0]` | `a zero-length array carries nothing and has no C or Python declaration` |
| `struct Stamped<T> { .. }`, `struct Borrowed<'a> { .. }` | `` a wire type has no type or lifetime parameter: whether it has padding would depend on the argument, and the witness would exist before that was checked. Write the struct for the one type it carries; a `const` parameter is allowed. `` |
| a field named `register`, `from` or `r#struct`; a type named `None` | `` `register` is a keyword of C, C++ or Python: this field could not be declared in the definitions generated from this struct. Rename it. `` |
| a field named `__reserved` | `` `__reserved` starts with two underscores: C reserves such a name and Python rewrites it inside a class. Rename this field. `` |
| `#[wire_plain(unit = "m")]` | `` the only field attribute is `values(NAME = integer, ..)` `` |
| `values(REVERSE = -1)` | `a named value is a plain non-negative integer: it is printed as an unsigned constant in C and Python` |

| `unsafe impl WirePlain for Range {}` | ``E0046 not all trait items implemented, missing: `LAYOUT` `` |
| `const TICKS: Topic<u32, KernelLane> = Topic::new(..)`, and `[u64; 6]` | `` a topic carries a record: a bare scalar or array has no field name for C or Python to read it by. Wrap it in a `#[repr(C)]` struct that derives `WirePlain`. `` |

|---|---|

```rust
    pub ROVER {
        /// World-fixed and continuous; drifts without bound.
        ODOM,
        /// The body: origin on the wheel axis, x forward, y left, z up.
        BASE_LINK moves in ODOM,
        /// The front range sensor: 0.10 m ahead of the wheel axis, turned 15 degrees left.
```

| Written | Is |
|---|---|
| `ODOM` | the root: the one frame with no parent |
| `BASE_LINK moves in ODOM` | a moving link: its pose in the parent is supplied each release |
| `RANGE_FRONT in BASE_LINK at { x: 0.10, yaw: Angle::from_degrees(15.0) }` | a mount: `x`, `y`, `z` in metres and `roll`, `pitch`, `yaw` as an `Angle`, each zero when omitted |

| Written | Error |

| `PLATE in SONAR at { .. }` and `SONAR in PLATE at { .. }` | `frames!: every frame's parents must lead to the root` |
| `RANGE_FRONT in BASE_LNK at { .. }`, a parent never declared | ``cannot find value `BASE_LNK` in this scope`` |
| `BASE_LINK` declared twice | ``the name `BASE_LINK` is defined multiple times`` |
| no bare name, or two: `ODOM` and `MAP` | `frames!: a frame set has exactly one root` |
| `yaw: 15.0` | ``expected `Angle`, found floating-point number`` |
| a frame of another robot's set given to `lookup` | ``the trait bound `Frame<rover::__Frames>: From<Frame<arm::__Frames>>` is not satisfied`` |
| a frame of another robot's set named as a parent, by a mount or by a moving frame: `GRIPPER in BASE_LINK at { .. }` in the arm's set, with the rover's `BASE_LINK` imported | ``expected `arm::__Frames`, found `rover::__Frames` `` |

```
[   10.704226] [FAIL] periodic upstream: could not start: topic `orphan/input` never appeared
[   10.712284] [FAIL] periodic upstream: its publication `orphan/output` is left without a writer
```

Why a node ended: it could not start, or the overrun policy stopped it after it had been
running. Either way the node writes ERROR records to the system log — its name, then one
phrase — and exits with status 1. Those two lines are the console of
`periodic_orphaned_publication` on QEMU raspi3b: a node that had created its publication
and then waited ten seconds for an input nobody publishes.

The text opens with the phase, so a node that ran for an hour before missing a deadline
never reads as one that failed to start. A node that cannot reach its topic says which and
why; it does not run forever reading `None`. Without a log service in the image, the
records go straight to the console.

**Where a node's records go.** The framework registers the node's log ring before its
first release, so each record it writes — an overrun, a run of refused publishes, why it
stopped — is one write into that ring, which `logview -s periodic` reads, after the node is
gone too. Writing one never makes a cycle wait for the log service. If `log_server` comes
up after the node, the node does not wait for it: its records go to the console until
`log_server` answers, and a thread of the node's own registers the ring within 2 s of the
node's start; a record written before then is on the console and not in the ring. Without
a log service in the image every record goes to the console.

| Why the node ended | `NodeError` | The record, after `<node>: ` |
|---|---|---|
| `every` is not a duration | `BadDuration { key: DurationKey::Every, text }` | ``could not start: `every` is `20 ms`, not a duration`` |
| an input's `stale_after` is not a duration | `BadDuration { key: DurationKey::StaleAfter(topic), text }` | ``could not start: `stale_after` of `sensor/range` is `70 ms`, not a duration`` |
| the period is zero, or rounds to zero ticks | `UnusablePeriod` | `could not start: the period rounds to zero ticks on this clock` |
| a topic still had no publisher when the budget ran out | `NeverAppeared(topic)` | ``could not start: topic `sensor/range` never appeared`` |
| the transport refused the open; waiting will not fix it | `Refused(topic, TopicError)` | ``could not start: topic `sensor/range` refused the open: `` and the transport's reason |
| the served action's `lease` is not a duration, in a call written by hand (the attribute refuses one at build time) | `BadDuration { key: DurationKey::Lease, text }` | ``could not start: `lease` is `100 ms`, not a duration`` |
| the served action's lease is shorter than twice the period | `LeaseTooShort { lease, every }` | `could not start: lease 39ms is shorter than twice the period 20ms` |
| a topic of the served action could not be opened, or its idle status not published | `ActionRefused { action, topic, reason }` | `could not start: action drive_to: drive_to/__goal: ` and the reason in a few words: `topic storage full`, `held by another definition`, `no seat free`, `name too long`, or the transport's own |
| the `Fault` policy stopped it | `DeadlineMissed(overruns)` | `stopped: missed 2 release(s) under on_overrun = Fault` |

A failed start is a `NodeFailure`: the `NodeError`, and each of the node's outputs it had
created before a later output, an input or its action failed. The outputs open first, in
declaration order, so a node with outputs `cmd/velocity` and `drive/state` whose input
never appears writes three records:

```
drive: could not start: topic `odometry` never appeared
drive: its publication `cmd/velocity` is left without a writer
drive: its publication `drive/state` is left without a writer
```

| Item | Is |
|---|---|
| `NodeFailure::reason()` | the `NodeError` |
| `NodeFailure::orphaned_publications()` | the outputs left without a writer, in declaration order; empty when there are none |
| `NodeFailure::records()` | `FailureRecord::Ended(reason)`, then one `FailureRecord::Orphaned(topic)` per output left without a writer: one log record each |
| `NodeFailure`'s `Display` | those records joined by `"; "`, for a surface with room for one sentence |

**One record per fact, not one sentence.** A record of the system log holds 96 bytes beside
the `periodic` tag, and a sentence naming the node, the topic that never appeared and the
publication left behind is longer than that. Each record leads with its names. Limits:

- **A refused-open record can be cut.** Its tail is the transport's own reason. A
  kernel-lane payload mismatch carries the shape in force, up to 98 bytes:
  ``estimator: could not start: topic `imu/data` refused the open: this is not the
  payload type the topic carries: it carries 48-byte payloads of layout 0x38793118`` is
  159 bytes and loses the end of the reason, and with it the shape, whatever the names.
  Both names survive. The `NodeError` carries the whole reason.
- **A mistyped-duration record fits while the node's name, the topic and the text are
  together 36 bytes or fewer.** Past that it loses its end, never the key or the start of
  the topic.
- **"Left without a writer" is said of every output created whenever something after it
  fails.** On the kernel lane, which takes several writers, another writer of that topic
  may be alive.
- **A publisher the program opened itself is not named** (see [Raw ends](#raw-ends)).

Two more records come from a node that is still running:

| Record | Level | When |
|---|---|---|
| `<node>: missed 2 release(s)` | WARNING | after each cycle that was handed an overrun count |
| `<node>: 16 consecutive publishes to <topic> refused (<reason>); still trying` | ERROR | once per run of refused publishes on that output, on the sixteenth; not again until a publish on it succeeds or it is declined. Each output keeps its own run, so two outputs can each report on one release. A C or Python node writes this record, in these words, to the console and not to its log ring, so `logview` does not show it there; its run also ends at a cycle that does not publish that output |

The reason in the second is the transport's. On the safe lane a publication the kernel
refused, an element it could not hand out included, is `Refused`; `BadShape` there means
only an element too small for the payload (`library/tail_core/src/topic/zero_copy.rs:222-227`),
which an output opened for its shape never meets. Read from the source, not reproduced.

A node's body runs exactly once on every release, whatever the transports answer to its
outputs' publishes, and a refusal on one output does not stop the others.

This is the Python half of [the Rust API](periodic_framework_public.md). The words mean
the same things and are spelled the same way, so a reader of that page already knows this
one. Where the two differ, this page says why.

A node reads as many topics as its body has inputs, each with its own bound, takes any
run-time parameters an operator tunes from the shell while it runs, serves at most one
[action](#actions) -- a goal a client sends it, which takes many releases -- and publishes
as many topics as its body has outputs, each on the releases the body chooses.

Four programs: a node that only publishes, a node that reads one topic, a node that
reads two, and a node that publishes two. None writes a loop or a sleep, and none declares a payload: each imports the
standard ones from `tail_messages`, which the build prints from the Rust crate
`robot_messages`, so a Python node and a Rust or C node hold one definition.

nothing to install, and `import periodic` loads it from `/usr/lib/python314.zip`.
`tail_messages` is a file of its own on the image, `/usr/lib/python3.14/tail_messages.py`,
printed by the image build. Python is on the disk image of the

```python
SENSOR_RANGE = Topic("sensor/range", Range, lane="safe")
```

A topic is defined once: its name, the payload it carries, and the lane that carries it.
All three belong to the topic and not to a node, because every end of a topic must agree on
them and one node may touch several topics that differ in each. A payload carries no frame:
the frame belongs to the topic, and its comment says which.

`examples/publisher.py`:

```python
from periodic import periodic, publish, run, monotonic_ns, Skip, Topic
from tail_messages import Range, RANGE_INFRARED

# The front ranger's readings, in the `range_front` frame.
FROM_PYTHON = Topic("pair/from_python", Range, lane="kernel")

count = 0


@periodic(every="20ms", on_overrun=Skip)
def sensor(reading=publish(FROM_PYTHON)):
    global count
    count += 1
    reading.publish(Range.instance(stamp_ns=monotonic_ns(), radiation_type=RANGE_INFRARED,
                                   field_of_view=0.05, min_range=0.02, max_range=4.0,
                                   range=0.25 * count, variance=0.0))


run()
```

An output is declared on the parameter that publishes it: `reading=publish(FROM_PYTHON)`.
On every release the body is handed an `Out` in that parameter, and `reading.publish(value)`
hands it the release's value; the framework publishes it once the body returns. A body
returns nothing. `count` lives at module level, which is one way
a Python node keeps state between cycles; [below](#init-has-no-equivalent-and-does-not-need-one)
is why Python needs no `init` for that. `monotonic_ns()` is the stamp clock: nanoseconds
since boot on the counter the node's releases are placed on, the clock every `stamp_ns`
field is in, and the same one `periodic::monotonic_ns()` reads in Rust and
`tail_periodic_monotonic_ns()` in C. `RANGE_INFRARED` is one of `Range`'s named values,
generated beside it.

There are two ways to read that clock, and they differ in a
[replay](#recording-and-replay):

| Call | What it returns | In a replay | Stamp with it |
|---|---|---|---|
| `monotonic_ns()` | the counter, read when called | a new reading, so what it stamps diverges | a measurement, when it is taken: this sensor node |
| `now()` | the release's reading: the instant every input of the release was judged against; 0 before `run()` has opened the node | the recorded reading, so what it stamps replays exactly | a value the node decides from its inputs |

`now()` is `periodic::now()` in Rust and `tail_periodic_now_ns(node)` in C. A process is
one node, so it takes none. Call it from the body: from a thread you started it raises
`RuntimeError`.

```python
    reading = lidar.get()
    # `get()` is None when nothing has arrived yet and when what last arrived is older than
    # `stale_after`. The two collapse on purpose, so this is the fail-safe branch.
    if reading is None:
        return
```
